content.text: Here is the summary of the deployment design doc. The rollout is split into three phases. Phase one provisions the new inference hosts behind the feature flag, mirrors five percent of production traffic to them, and compares latency histograms nightly. Phase two widens the mirror to half of all traffic, enables the write path against the shadow store, and adds the reconciliation job that flags any divergence between the two stores within fifteen minutes. Phase three flips the flag for all tenants, keeps the old fleet warm for two weeks as a rollback target, and then decommissions it. The main open risks called out are cache warm-up time after the flip and the unbounded backlog the reconciliation job could accumulate if divergence is persistent rather than transient.

The capacity section says the new fleet is sized for peak plus forty percent headroom. Each inference host carries two replicas of the model server, pinned to separate NUMA nodes, with the router weighting requests by observed p99 latency rather than round robin. The failure-mode table covers three scenarios: a single host loss (absorbed by headroom, no action), an availability-zone loss (router drains the zone and pages the on-call), and a full regional failover (manual runbook, forty-five minute target). The doc recommends rehearsing the regional failover once a quarter and wiring the drain procedure into the deploy tooling so an operator can trigger it with one command instead of editing routing tables by hand during an incident.

The doc does not give a hard date — it gates the flag flip on two clean weeks of reconciliation, which the timeline sketch puts in early September.
